title: Sequence and conditionals
objective: Derive weakest preconditions for sequences, conditionals and guarded commands, name the reading of a guard, and derive Transfer's weakest precondition by hand.

segments.title: Rules for sequence, branch and guard

choice.prompt: Transfer is `requires g; move`, where `g` is `bal(from) ≥ amount`. Which formula is `wp(Transfer, Q)` for a state predicate `Q`?

options.why: This treats a rejected command as an abort: with `g` required, the `¬g` conjunct never applies. Mini-Plinth does not abort: it returns `Err` and leaves the state alone.
This treats a failing guard as a run that does not count. A rejected command does run, and the unchanged state must satisfy `Q`.
A successful move must establish `Q`, and the rejected, unchanged state must already satisfy it.
This ignores the guard on the branch that moves.

blocks.md:
Two rules cover sequence and branching. Work backwards through a sequence, last command first, and split a branch by its condition:

`wp(c₁; c₂, Q) = wp(c₁, wp(c₂, Q))`

`wp(if b then c₁ else c₂, Q) = (b → wp(c₁, Q)) ∧ (¬b → wp(c₂, Q))`

A guard `g` before a body `c` has four readings. They differ in what a failing guard means:

| Reading | When `g` fails | `wp(g; c, Q)` |
|---|---|---|
| `if g → c fi` (Dijkstra) | the program aborts | `g ∧ wp(c, Q)` |
| `assert g; c` | an error to rule out | `g ∧ wp(c, Q)` |
| `assume g; c` | the run is ignored | `g → wp(c, Q)` |
| `requires g; c` (Mini-Plinth) | `Err`, state unchanged | `(g → wp(c, Q)) ∧ (¬g → Q)` |

The first two share a formula and differ in meaning. Mini-Plinth is the last row: a rejected command still runs and leaves the state as it was, so `Q` must already hold there. One cost to know: the weakest precondition of n sequential `if`s copies `Q` up to 2ⁿ times, because each branch substitutes into its own copy. Naming each intermediate formula with `define-fun` keeps the query linear, and LAB-4.3 tests it.[^1]

[^1]: Drawer D-10 maps the notation of Programming Language Foundations onto this one.

blocks.direction: Query asserts: for each line, a state where the line fails to follow from what it rests on. Line 5 asks for a state where the assume-reading candidate and the reject-reading formula disagree. `sat` means the line is not valid.

code.text:
command  Transfer:  requires amount ≤ a;  a := a − amount;  b := b + amount
post     Inv = a ≥ 0 ∧ b ≥ 0

1  wp(b := b + amount, Inv)         =  a ≥ 0 ∧ b + amount ≥ 0                          rule: assignment
2  wp(a := a − amount; …, Inv)      =  a − amount ≥ 0 ∧ b + amount ≥ 0                 rule: sequence, then assignment
3  wp(requires …, Inv)              =  (amount ≤ a → line 2) ∧ (¬(amount ≤ a) → Inv)   rule: guard, reject reading
4  candidate, assume reading        =  amount ≤ a → line 2                             rule: guard, assume reading
5  line 4  ⇔  line 3                                                                   rule: equivalence

call.prompt: Is the assume-reading candidate (line 4) equivalent to the reference weakest precondition of Transfer (line 3)?

options.text: They are equivalent formulas in every state of the model.
options.why: This treats a false antecedent as irrelevant. When the guard fails, the reject reading still asks the unchanged state to satisfy Inv.

options.text: They differ wherever the guard fails, whatever Inv says.
options.why: If the guard fails and Inv holds, both formulas are true. The difference needs one more condition.

options.text: They differ only where the guard fails and Inv already fails.
options.why: There the assume reading says nothing, and the reject reading asks the unchanged state to satisfy Inv, which it does not.

blocks.after: Where the guard holds, both formulas reduce to the same thing. They part only in a state that breaks Inv before the command runs and fails the guard. {{run:RUN-z3-wp-transfer}}

blocks.md: Once Z3 finds your hand-derived `wp(Transfer, Inv)` equivalent to the reference, this page mints claim CL-4.1. It covers the formula, not the code that will run.

choice.prompt: The command is `assert amount ≤ limit; a := a − amount` with postcondition `a ≥ 0`. A failing `assert` is an error to rule out. Which formula is the weakest precondition?

options.why: This is the assume reading, which lets a failing guard off. A failing `assert` is an error.
This is the reject reading, which runs a failed guard and keeps the state. An `assert` has no such run.
The guard must hold, and the body must establish the postcondition.

choice.prompt: Which formula is the weakest precondition of `if a ≥ amount then a := a − amount else b := b + amount` for `a ≥ 0 ∧ b ≥ 0`?

options.text: `(a ≥ amount → a − amount ≥ 0 ∧ b ≥ 0) ∧ (a < amount → a ≥ 0 ∧ b + amount ≥ 0)`
options.why: Each branch gets its own weakest precondition, under its own condition.

options.text: `(a ≥ amount → a − amount ≥ 0 ∧ b ≥ 0) ∧ (a < amount → true)`
options.why: This drops the else branch, so it says nothing when `a < amount`.
This requires both branches to work, whatever the condition says.

options.text: `(a ≥ amount → a ≥ 0 ∧ b + amount ≥ 0) ∧ (a < amount → a − amount ≥ 0 ∧ b ≥ 0)`
options.why: This pairs each condition with the other branch's weakest precondition.

blocks.title: Reading
blocks.md: Read 2026-10-23: [Programming Language Foundations](https://softwarefoundations.cis.upenn.edu/plf-current/), chapter Hoare, "Proof Rules" (Sequencing, Conditionals) and "Additional Exercises" (Assert and Assume); chapter Hoare2, "Weakest Preconditions (Optional)". Optional: Dijkstra's 1975 paper on guarded commands, the sections that define the statements and their weakest preconditions.

blocks.md: Extend your emitter to conditionals and guards, all four readings, and keep a chain of twelve `if`s small enough to check.

notes: The three cells are plain-text derivations for the Derivation Board (INS-derivation), which is not built yet; wp_transfer.py states each line as the cells' @direction describes it, and the cells are committed verbatim beside it.

In S4.L2 cell 2 the post bal(x) + bal(y) + bal(z) = S is a formula in a free S, so "the weakest preconditions disagree" is a state and an S where one sum equals S and the other does not; x, y and z are not assumed distinct. S4.L2 cell 2's @call cites RUN-z3-selftransfer; its instrument cites this run.
S4.L3 cell 1 states no amount > 0, so none is assumed; the disagreement's witness may have amount = 0.
